extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, agents, and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from the MPEP for applying AIA prior-art exceptions, use of affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.130, joint research agreement rules, and related patentability (novelty/obviousness) considerations under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) prior-art exception (inventor/public disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is required for subject matter in the intervening U.S. patent document to be excepted under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) is that the subject matter must have been previously publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor (or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no requirement that the mode of prior disclosure by the inventor (or another who obtained the subject matter from the inventor) be the same as the mode of disclosure of the intervening U.S. patent document (e.g., patenting, publication, public use, sale activity). The prior disclosure need not be verbatim; differing words or modes do not preclude the exception. The exception applies only to the subject matter in the intervening document that was previously publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial-coverage effect of 102(b)(2)(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor or a joint inventor had publicly disclosed elements A, B, and C, and a subsequent intervening U.S. patent document discloses elements A, B, C, and D, then only element D of the intervening U.S. patent document is available as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking 102(b)(2)(B), examine which specific subject-matter elements were publicly disclosed earlier by the inventor; only the non-previously-disclosed elements of the intervening document remain available as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus/species treatment under 102(b)(2)(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If subject matter of an intervening U.S. patent document is simply a more general description of the subject matter previously publicly disclosed by the inventor (e.g., inventor disclosed a species and the intervening document discloses a genus), the exception in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) applies to such subject matter of the intervening U.S. patent document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inventor publicly disclosed a species and a later intervening document discloses a genus — the genus disclosure in the intervening document is not available as prior art. Conversely, if the inventor disclosed a genus and the intervening document discloses a species, that species in the intervening document would be available as prior art. If the intervening document discloses an alternative species not disclosed earlier by the inventor, that alternative species is prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of inquiry for 102(b)(2)(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of whether the exception in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B) is applicable to subject matter in an intervening U.S. patent document does not involve a comparison of the subject matter of the claimed invention to either the subject matter disclosed by the inventor or the subject matter of the subsequent intervening U.S. patent document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry is limited to whether the subject matter of the intervening document was previously publicly disclosed by the inventor (or someone who obtained it from the inventor). Whether the prior art anticipates or renders obvious the claimed invention is a separate inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) common ownership/obligation-of-assignment exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The exception disqualifies subject matter disclosed in a U.S. patent document from constituting prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, 'were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the conditions of 102(b)(2)(C) are met, the U.S. patent document may not be available as prior art under either AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103. This differs from pre-AIA 103(c). However, the exception does not apply to disclosures qualifying under 102(a)(1), and even if disqualified as prior art, such documents may still be used for double patenting, enablement, or to indicate state of the art where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on 102(b)(2)(C) — 102(a)(1), double patenting, enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) exception does not apply to a disclosure that qualifies as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) (disclosures made before the effective filing date of the claimed invention). Also, a double patenting rejection may still be made on the basis of the U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication, and such documents may be cited to indicate the state of the art for lack of enablement rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when common-ownership/assignment conditions are asserted, examiners should check for 102(a)(1) status (publication/issue dates) and consider double-patenting and enablement contexts separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR rules for commonly owned/joint research agreement subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office revised rules of practice to include provisions that pertain to commonly owned or joint research agreement subject matter (37 CFR 1.104(c)(4) and (c)(5)). 37 CFR 1.104(c)(4) applies to applications subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, and 37 CFR 1.104(c)(5) applies to pre-AIA cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should apply the appropriate CFR provision depending on whether the application is examined under AIA (FITF) or pre-AIA law. See MPEP § 706.02(l)(1) for treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement by applicant to establish common-ownership exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear and conspicuous statement by the applicant (or the applicant's representative of record) that the claimed invention and the subject matter disclosed in the U.S. patent document were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention will be sufficient to establish that the AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) exception applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may present supporting evidence such as assignment copies but is not required to do so. The Office will not request corroborating evidence in the absence of independent evidence raising doubt as to veracity. Statements under 102(b)(2)(C) are treated analogously to statements under pre-AIA 103(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.130(a) — affidavit/declaration of attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: When any claim is rejected, the applicant or patent owner may submit an appropriate affidavit or declaration to disqualify a disclosure as prior art by establishing that the disclosure was made by the inventor or a joint inventor, or the subject matter disclosed was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a mechanism to show authorship/origin of a disclosure so it can be excluded as prior art under the AIA exceptions (e.g., 102(b)(1)(A), 102(b)(2)(A)).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.130(b) — affidavit/declaration of prior public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When any claim is rejected, the applicant or patent owner may submit an affidavit or declaration to disqualify a disclosure as prior art by establishing that the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure was made or before such subject matter was effectively filed, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The affidavit/declaration must identify the subject matter publicly disclosed and provide the date such subject matter was publicly disclosed. If the earlier disclosure was a printed publication, a copy must accompany the affidavit (37 CFR 1.130(b)(1)). If not printed, describe the subject matter with sufficient detail and particularity to determine what was publicly disclosed (37 CFR 1.130(b)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and procedural limits on 37 CFR 1.130
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions of 37 CFR 1.130 are not available if the rejection is based upon a disclosure made more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention. The provisions may not be available if the rejection is based upon a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication naming another inventor where the patent/pending application claims the same or substantially the same invention and the affidavit contends derivation by that inventor, in which case a derivation proceeding may be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the disclosure predates the effective filing date by more than one year, it is prior art under 102(a)(1) and cannot be disqualified under 102(b)(1). If derivation is alleged, consider petitions for derivation under 37 CFR 42.401 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability scope for 37 CFR 1.130
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions of 37 CFR 1.130 apply to any application (and patents issuing thereon) that contains, or contained at any time, a claim to a claimed invention that has an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, or a specific reference under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) to any patent or application that contains such a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check effective filing date and specific references to determine whether 1.130 relief is available in the case under examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of proof/evidence for 37 CFR 1.130(a) attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the authorship of the prior art disclosure includes the inventor or a joint inventor named in the application, an 'unequivocal' statement from the inventor or joint inventor that the inventor or joint inventor (or specific combination of named inventors) invented the subject matter of the disclosure, accompanied by a reasonable explanation of the presence of additional authors, may be acceptable in the absence of evidence to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere statement without reasonable explanation may be insufficient when evidence to the contrary exists. See case references (In re Katz; In re DeBaun; Ex parte Kroger) cited for analogous situations; examiners should weigh contrary evidence when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for 37 CFR 1.130(b) prior-public-disclosure affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner of disclosure of subject matter referenced in an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130(b)(2) is not critical; any manner of disclosure that renders a claimed invention 'available to the public' may be evidenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the subject matter have been disclosed in the same manner or using the same words. Example: inventor publicly disclosed subject matter via a slide presentation at a scientific meeting, while intervening disclosure was in a journal article — differences in manner or words do not preclude use of 1.130(b) to disqualify the intervening disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130
rubrics_metrics.description: In accordance with 37 CFR 1.130, the applicant or patent owner may submit an affidavit or declaration. When an assignee, obligated assignee, or person showing sufficient proprietary interest is the applicant under 35 U.S.C. 118 rather than the inventor, the inventor may sign an affidavit or declaration but it must be filed by a party having authority to take action in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority to file papers generally does not lie with the inventor if the inventor is not the applicant. Ensure the affidavit/declaration is filed by a party with proper authority in the application record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations making 37 CFR 1.130 unavailable (derivation and double-patenting risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.130 is not available if the rejection is based upon a disclosure made more than one year before the effective filing date. The provisions may also not be available if the rejection is based upon a U.S. patent/application naming another inventor and the affidavit contends derivation, or if applying 1.130 would result in issuance/confirmation of two patents containing patentably indistinct claims to two different parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such situations, applicants may file a petition for a derivation proceeding (37 CFR 42.401 et seq.). Consider In re Deckler regarding the principle that only one patent should issue for inventions that are identical or not patentably distinct when different inventive entities are concerned.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) joint research agreement conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person in applying subsection (b)(2)(C) if: (1) the subject matter disclosed was developed and the claimed invention was made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the application for patent discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'joint research agreement' is a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement by two or more persons/entities for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention. If these three conditions are met, the joint research agreement prior art is not available as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoking joint research agreement — procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To invoke a joint research agreement to disqualify a disclosure as prior art, the applicant (or representative) must provide a statement that the disclosure and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement, that the agreement was in effect on or before the effective filing date, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the names of the parties to the joint research agreement are not stated in the application, the application must be amended to include the names in accordance with 37 CFR 1.71(g). The applicant may but is not required to present supporting evidence; the Office will not request corroboration absent independent doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship/naming requirement and corrective procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent laws require naming the actual inventor or joint inventors of the claimed subject matter (35 U.S.C. 115(a)). The Office presumes the named inventor(s) are correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an application names incorrect inventorship, the applicant should submit a request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48. In rare situations where the application clearly does not name the correct inventorship and no correction is filed, Office personnel should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115. Do not make a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) if the application is subject to FITF provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 — effective filing date and claim-focused differences
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 continues to set forth the nonobviousness requirement, but AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 determines obviousness as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention (rather than as of the time the invention was made). AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 requires consideration of 'the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice during examination, this distinction only matters when the case is subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 and evidence of an invention date prior to the effective filing date exists (often shown by affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131). The term 'claims' has been used historically to define the invention believed patentable; apply Graham factors and ascertain differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
